newsitem.title: CZECH REPUBLIC: Analysts disappointed as Czech GDP growth slows.
newsitem.headline: Analysts disappointed as Czech GDP growth slows.

text.p: Czech gross domestic product growth slowed in the second quarter, sending some disappointed analysts scrambling to revise downward their full year forecasts.

The Czech Statistical Bureau (CSU) on Wednesday released figures showing real Czech economic growth for the second quarter slowed to 4.0 percent year-on-year, after 4.6 percent growth in the first quarter.
Analysts said they were disappointed with the figures that compared unfavourably with neighbouring countries such as Slovakia, which posted second-quarter growth of just under seven percent.

"It is worse than expected, but there are some obvious factors such as the relatively bad performance of the external sector (exports) and the deceleration of industrial production and construction output," said Zdenek Tuma, chief economist at investment bank Patria Finance.
Tuma said he saw little room for a pick-up in growth in the second half, adding Patria would revise its forecast for full-year growth from the current range of 5.0-5.5 to below five percent.
Analysts partly attributed the turnaround to sluggish performances by many of the Czech Republic's major trading partners in the European Union.
Some also said the government should do more to boost exports.

"I think we are living in a European environment. Q2 (Second quarter) was perhaps influenced by a slowing of exports, and export support could be improved," said Kamil Janacek, chief economist at the country's largest commercial bank, Komercni Banka.

Charlie Robinson, an analyst at the London-based investment house Hilfe, said some of the figures such as a narrowing of the gap between imports and exports of goods and services and a decrease in aggregate demand, were encouraging signs the Czech National Bank (CNB) may have room to cut interest rates.
"The figures seem to suggest that the central bank may be able to cut interest rates. Its high interest rate policy may not be so necessary," he said.
In June, the CNB raised the discount rate to 10.5 percent from 9.5 percent to curb inflation.
Year-on-year inflation in August was 9.6 percent, which though lower than in many neighbouring countries, has proven stubbornly resistant to any further decline.
On Monday, Prime Minister Vaclav Klaus, a monetarist economist, appeared to rule out any slackening of moneteray policy until inflation dropped further.
